Pillar 1 of 5 · الشهادة Shahada — The Declaration of Faith The first and foundational pillar of Islam: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad ﷺ is His messenger. أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ The Shahada "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Foundation What is the Shahada? The Shahada (شَهَادَة, meaning "testimony") is the Islamic declaration of faith and the first of the Five Pillars of Islam. It consists of two inseparable clauses — Tawhid (the oneness of God) and Risala (the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ). Pronouncing the Shahada with sincere belief and understanding is the entry point into Islam. It is the foundation upon which all other acts of worship stand. A person who dies believing in the Shahada is promised admission to Paradise (Sahih Bukhari 128). Sahih Bukhari 128 · Sahih Muslim 26 "Whoever dies knowing that there is no god but Allah will enter Paradise." — The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ (narrated by Uthman ibn Affan RA) The Two Clauses Understanding each part لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ Lā ilāha illallāh There is no god but Allah. This is Tawhid — the absolute oneness and uniqueness of God. It negates all false deities and affirms that worship belongs to Allah alone. مُحَمَّدٌ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ Muhammadun Rasūlullāh Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. This is Risala — the affirmation of prophethood. It means accepting the Qur'an as revelation and Muhammad ﷺ as the seal of all prophets. Conditions of Validity Seven conditions for the Shahada to be accepted Scholars have extracted seven conditions from the Qur'an and Sunnah that must be met for the Shahada to be valid — mere pronunciation without these is insufficient. عِلْم1. KnowledgeKnowing what the Shahada affirms and denies — understanding Tawhid.يَقِين2. CertaintyAbsolute conviction, free from doubt or wavering.إِخْلَاص3. SincerityPure intention for Allah alone, not for status or worldly gain.صِدْق4. TruthfulnessThe heart aligning with what the tongue declares.مَحَبَّة5. LoveLoving Allah, His Messenger, and the obligations that come with the Shahada.اِنْقِيَاد6. SubmissionOutward compliance and submission to the implications of the declaration.قَبُول7. AcceptanceEmbracing everything the Shahada entails without rejection.Tawhid — Divine Oneness The three dimensions of Tawhid قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ ۝ اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُQur'an 112:1–2 "Say: He is Allah, [who is] One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge." — Surah Al-Ikhlas, described by the Prophet ﷺ as equal to one-third of the Qur'an in meaning (Sahih Bukhari 5013).1Tawhid al-Rububiyyah — Oneness of LordshipThe belief that Allah alone is the Creator, Sustainer, and Sovereign of all existence. No partner shares in His dominion.2Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah — Oneness of WorshipAll acts of worship — prayer, supplication, sacrifice, hope, fear, love — belong exclusively to Allah. Directing any of these to other than Allah is shirk.3Tawhid al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat — Oneness of Names & AttributesAllah's 99 names and attributes are affirmed as He described them in the Qur'an and Sunnah — without distortion, negation, asking how, or likening to creation.Common Questions FAQ Can non-Muslims say the Shahada? +Yes — saying the Shahada with sincere belief is what makes a person Muslim. There is no formal ceremony required, though it is recommended to do so in front of witnesses. Ghusl (ritual bath) is recommended after conversion.Does the Shahada need to be in Arabic? +The majority scholarly position is that understanding the meaning is essential, but the Arabic pronunciation is preferred as the authoritative form. Most scholars permit saying it in one's language initially, with learning the Arabic encouraged.What is shirk (association)? +Shirk is the act of associating partners with Allah in worship, lordship, or attributes — the opposite of Tawhid. The Qur'an describes it as the only sin that is not forgiven if one dies upon it without repentance (4:48).How many prophets were there? +The Qur'an mentions 25 prophets by name. Hadith literature mentions 124,000 prophets were sent throughout history. Muhammad ﷺ is the last and final prophet — no prophet comes after him.Go deeper The Six Articles of Faith (Arkan al-Iman) Alongside the Shahada, a Muslim must hold six fundamental beliefs — the pillars of Iman defined in the Hadith of Jibril. They cover belief in Allah, the angels, the revealed scriptures, the prophets, the Day of Judgement, and divine decree (Qadr). أركان الإيمانThe Six Articles of Faith A full in-depth guide to each article — with Qur'anic evidence, scholarly explanation, and key points for each belief.
